item.text:
Below is a text-based issue list, not a conclusion that any particular course of conduct would be lawful. **Some provisions create express exceptions; others create uncertainty that agencies or courts could resolve against an operator.** I cannot guarantee an exhaustive list without the surrounding statutory framework, legislative history, and implementing rules.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **§ 2(1)—“Artificial intelligence” is undefined.** The text provides no boundary between an AI model or system and conventional software, statistical tools, or hybrid products, leaving the basic scope of coverage uncertain.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Strict compute threshold.** “Greater than” excludes a training run using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations, and compute below that threshold is not independently covered by this prong. Such systems could nevertheless qualify under § 2(1)(B).

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” is undefined.** The bill does not specify whether pretraining, continued training, fine-tuning, restarts, or distributed training constitute one run or several. It supplies no aggregation rule for related training stages.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute measurement is unspecified.** The text does not identify how to count operations, including mixed-precision calculations, sparsity, recomputation, unsuccessful runs, or auxiliary models. It also provides no measurement standard, recordkeeping requirement, or verification process.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Training compute excludes other sources of capability.** Inference-time computation, tool use, retrieval, and system-level orchestration are not expressly counted toward the threshold. Coverage of capabilities produced through these mechanisms therefore depends on the separate capability determination.

6. **§ 2(1)—Relationship between a model and a system is unclear.** Prong (A) covers a “model,” while prong (B) covers a “system,” without explaining how coverage transfers to derivatives, distilled models, ensembles, or products incorporating a covered component. This creates uncertainty about what downstream development or deployment is prohibited.

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill names the Secretary of State elsewhere and assigns Commerce registry duties, but never defines which Secretary makes capability determinations. That omission leaves the decisionmaker’s authority uncertain.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—Capability standard lacks objective benchmarks.** “Substantially,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” are undefined. The text does not establish the relevant human comparison group, task universe, evaluation conditions, or treatment of uneven performance.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage appears dependent on an affirmative determination.** Unlike prong (A), prong (B) describes systems that the Secretary “determines” possess the specified capability. The text does not say whether otherwise qualifying systems are covered before such a determination or whether determinations can apply retrospectively.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure.** There are no requirements for notice, evidence, publication, timing, reconsideration, or administrative review. Ordinary administrative-law protections may apply, but the bill supplies no tailored process for this consequential designation.

11. **§ 2(1)—Compute and capability are independent triggers.** A high-compute model can be prohibited even if incapable of exceptional performance, while a lower-compute highly capable system requires a Secretary’s determination. This mismatch makes the scope dependent partly on resource consumption and partly on administrative action rather than one consistent capability standard.

12. **§ 2(2)—“U.S. person” excludes several common categories.** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and does not expressly include partnerships, LLCs, trusts, unincorporated associations, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions matter principally to the prohibition’s overseas reach; persons operating within the United States remain subject to its territorial limb.

13. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign affiliates are not expressly attributed to U.S. parents.** The bill contains no ownership, control, agency, or attribution rule for foreign-organized entities. A parent’s own prohibited conduct could still be covered, and other applicable liability doctrines should not be assumed away.

14. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** The registry threshold lacks specifications for performance, architecture, intended use, or equivalent hardware. Whether general-purpose accelerators or future chip designs count is therefore uncertain.

15. **§ 2(3)—Facility boundaries and chip counting are unspecified.** The text does not explain whether a campus, building, tenant’s installation, or linked group of data centers constitutes one facility, or whether inactive and spare chips count. “More than 50,000” also excludes exactly 50,000 chips.

16. **§§ 2(1), 2(3), 4—Registry coverage does not track prohibited-system coverage.** A covered model could be trained outside a covered facility, while a covered facility could run no prohibited workloads. The registry therefore is neither a complete inventory of covered AI activity nor limited to facilities undertaking it.

### Prohibition and exceptions

17. **§ 3(a)—“Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are undefined.** The text does not distinguish research, testing, fine-tuning, hosting, commercial release, maintenance, or ordinary use. “Develop” is particularly open-ended and may overlap substantially with both other verbs.

18. **§§ 2(1)(A), 3(a)—Timing of coverage during training is unclear.** A model may not satisfy the compute definition until a run crosses the threshold, yet training that model is the prohibited conduct. The text does not state how planned training, threshold-crossing, or conduct before crossing is treated.

19. **§ 3(a)—Possession and ordinary use are not expressly prohibited.** The listed verbs do not explicitly include possessing weights, downloading a model, distributing it, or using its outputs. Whether particular conduct falls within “develop” or “deploy” remains a separate question.

20. **§ 3(a)—Geographic attachment is uncertain for remote activity.** The bill does not specify how to locate conduct involving a user, developer, cloud operator, and hardware in different countries. “Any person in the United States” could generate disputes over whether location refers to the actor, infrastructure, or relevant act.

21. **§ 3(a)—No express allocation of responsibility across participants.** The text does not distinguish developers, infrastructure providers, hosts, contractors, customers, and distributors. It leaves uncertain when providing services constitutes direct prohibited conduct, although generally applicable criminal participation doctrines may still matter.

22. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering has no completion deadline.** The exception applies to a covered system whose training “began” before enactment, without requiring completion before enactment or within a subsequent period. On its face, it could exempt continuing training long after the statute takes effect.

23. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering extends beyond training.** Because the exception disapplies all of subsection (a), it appears to permit development and deployment of qualifying pre-enactment systems, not merely completion of their training. There is no express restriction on their later commercial deployment.

24. **§ 3(b)—“Training began” lacks a substantive commencement standard.** The text does not prescribe meaningful progress, minimum computation, documentation, or continuity requirements. Disputes could arise over whether preliminary or nominal activity establishes grandfathered status.

25. **§ 3(b)—System identity after modification is undefined.** The bill does not say when additional training, architectural changes, new components, or capability improvements produce a new system rather than continue an exempt one. This uncertainty affects how far grandfathering extends to later versions and derivatives.

26. **§§ 3(b), 8—Grandfathering cutoff precedes effectiveness.** Systems first trained during the 180-day interval after enactment are not grandfathered, although the prohibition is not yet effective. The text supplies no transition rule for winding down or handling systems lawfully begun during that interval.

27. **§ 3(c)—Safety-evaluation exception is broad.** The exception applies to “activities” conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation without defining that purpose or limiting which training, development, or deployment activities qualify. It contains no express necessity, proportionality, or containment requirement.

28. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The text does not specify whether safety evaluation must be the sole, primary, or merely one genuine purpose. It also does not distinguish evaluation from capability-enhancing work performed during an evaluation.

29. **§ 3(c)—No approval, oversight, or exception-specific documentation.** The bill requires no evaluator qualification, advance authorization, reporting of findings, or records substantiating the exception. This creates an enforcement and proof problem, although invoking an exception would not necessarily eliminate an operator’s evidentiary burden.

### Registry and enforcement

30. **§ 4(a)—No registration deadline or procedure.** Operators must register, but the text sets no deadline for existing facilities or facilities that newly cross the threshold. It also does not prescribe registration contents, updates, or deregistration.

31. **§ 4—“Operator” and shared-facility obligations are undefined.** Responsibility is unclear where owners, tenants, cloud providers, and management contractors share control. The reporting provision also shifts from registering each facility to reports by each “registered operator,” leaving the reporting unit uncertain.

32. **§ 4(b)—Quarterly reporting requirements lack essential specifications.** The text does not define calendar versus rolling quarters, submission deadlines, workload detail, compute accounting, or certification standards. “Describing” workloads could yield reports too general to establish compliance.

33. **§§ 4, 5—No express penalties for registry violations.** Section 5 addresses violations of § 3 only, not failure to register, report, or certify accurately under § 4. Other laws or enforcement mechanisms might apply, but this bill creates no tailored registry penalty.

34. **§§ 2–5—No express investigatory or implementing framework.** The bill does not expressly provide inspection, subpoena, audit, testing, record-preservation, or rulemaking powers, or clearly identify the civil enforcement authority. Existing legal powers may fill some gaps, but the text itself does not establish a complete enforcement system.

35. **§ 5(a)—Civil penalty units are ambiguous.** “For each day” does not clarify whether separate models, activities, facilities, or actors generate multiple penalties on the same day. It also leaves uncertainty about when deployment becomes a continuing violation rather than a discrete act.

36. **§ 5(a)—No express civil culpability standard.** Civil liability is not conditioned on knowledge, recklessness, or negligence. Combined with uncertain definitions and changing capability determinations, this creates fair-notice concerns and potentially severe exposure for inadvertent violations.

37. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” is not elaborated.** The text does not specify whether criminal liability requires knowledge of illegality, knowledge of the facts establishing coverage, or some other showing. Courts would need to interpret the term in context, especially for disputed thresholds and capability designations.

38. **§§ 2, 3, 5(b)—Uncertain coverage has heightened criminal consequences.** Undefined technical boundaries, an open-ended capability standard, and unclear exceptions support potential fair-notice or vagueness challenges given the ten-year prison maximum. Such challenges are not automatically successful, particularly for conduct clearly within the statutory core.

39. **§§ 5(a), 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness by 180 days. The better harmonized reading may be that no § 3 violation exists before effectiveness, but the penalty language unnecessarily creates a retroactivity dispute.

### International provisions and duration

40. **§ 6—Negotiation deadline is unclear and does not require an agreement.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly distinguish beginning negotiations from completing them. It requires an effort, not foreign participation or a successful agreement.

41. **§ 6—“Equivalent” international prohibitions are unspecified.** The bill does not clarify whether equivalence includes grandfathering, safety exceptions, geographic reach, enforcement, or the sunset. Nor does it make the domestic prohibition conditional on securing equivalent foreign restrictions.

42. **§ 7(a)—No mechanism or deadline for the National Academies report.** The text neither directs the Academies to produce a report nor establishes commissioning, funding, scope, or timing. The early-termination mechanism therefore depends on a report the Act does not itself ensure will exist.

43. **§ 7(a)—Safety finding and congressional process are underspecified.** “Can be developed safely” supplies no acceptable-risk standard or distinction among covered systems. The text also provides no expedited procedure, and a joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential approval or a veto override.

44. **§ 7(a)—Ending the prohibition does not expressly end the rest of the Act.** An early safety finding addresses § 3, while registry duties and other provisions are not expressly terminated. The consequences for penalties already accrued and ongoing reporting should be clarified.

45. **§§ 7(b), 8—Sunset runs from enactment, not effectiveness.** The Act expires ten years after enactment despite taking effect 180 days later, producing an operative period of approximately nine and a half years. If ten years of operative restrictions were intended, the dates are misaligned.

46. **§ 7(b)—Sunset consequences are not specified.** The bill lacks an express savings or wind-down provision governing accrued penalties, pending proceedings, registry records, and outstanding reports. General statutory savings rules may preserve some liabilities, so expiration should not be assumed to erase prior violations.
